questions.title: Which UI5 debugging tools should you know: the UI5 Inspector, debug mode, and the diagnostics / support tools?
questions.description: UI5 offers several tools on top of the browser's developer tools. The UI5 Inspector is a browser extension (for Chrome and Edge) that adds a UI5 tab to the developer tools: it shows the control tree of the running app, and for the selected control its properties (which you can change live), aggregations, associations, and bindings (binding paths, models, and the binding context), highlights the control on the page, and shows app information like the UI5 version and loaded libraries. Debug mode loads the readable debug sources instead of the minified ones, so you can read the code and set breakpoints: add sap-ui-debug=true to the URL, or switch it on in the Technical Information dialog. That dialog opens with Ctrl+Alt+Shift+P: it shows the UI5 version, the loaded libraries and the app's configuration, lets you activate debug sources (for all or selected modules), and starts the Support Assistant. Ctrl+Alt+Shift+S opens the support (diagnostics) tool, with a control tree, properties, and debugging settings. The Support Assistant checks the running app against a set of rules (for performance, accessibility, deprecated APIs, binding errors and more) and reports issues with explanations; it can also be started with the URL parameter sap-ui-support=true. The two situations where the UI5 Inspector saves most time: an empty field (the data binding view shows the resolved path; usually the path is right and the value is missing, like a missing $expand, or the path is wrong, like a typo or a missing binding context) and the wrong model (the control tree shows which models a control really sees, which exposes a model propagation problem or a dialog without addDependent). The Support Assistant's rule sets cover best practices (wrong API usage, missing super calls), accessibility, performance (too many controls, avoidable requests), memory (controls never destroyed, handlers never detached) and deprecation (very useful before a UI5 2.x migration); it can start silently with sap-ui-support=true,silent, and its report can be exported for a support ticket. Running it once before a release is cheap and usually finds something. When someone reports a bug, the Technical Information dialog is the first screenshot to ask for.
keyPoints: UI5 Inspector (browser extension): control tree, live properties, bindings, models, and app info.
Debug mode: sap-ui-debug=true (or via Technical Information) loads readable debug sources.
Ctrl+Alt+Shift+P: Technical Information (version, libraries, debug sources, Support Assistant); Ctrl+Alt+Shift+S: diagnostics tool.
The Support Assistant checks the app against rules (performance, accessibility, deprecations).
Inspector: empty field → check resolved path; wrong model → check propagation / addDependent.
Support Assistant rule sets: best practice, accessibility, performance, memory, deprecation; export the report.

https://host/app/index.html?sap-ui-debug=my/app/       debug sources for the app only

questions.title: How do you debug at runtime through global access and get a control globally in the console?
questions.description: While debugging in the browser console, you often want to look at a control or a model of the running app. Inside the app's code, you always find controls through the view (this.byId) and never through globals. In the console, for debugging only, there are global ways in. sap.ui.core.Element.getElementById("fullId") (the modern API; the older sap.ui.getCore().byId is deprecated since UI5 1.119) returns a control by its full, prefixed ID, which you can copy from the DOM (the id attribute of the control's root element) or from the UI5 Inspector. Once you have a control, you can call its methods, like getText(), getBindingContext().getObject(), getModel().getData() for a JSONModel, or getBinding("items") to inspect a list binding. Another way is to select an element in the Elements panel and use its ID. Global modules can be reached with sap.ui.require("module/name") if they are already loaded, for example sap.ui.require("sap/ui/core/Element"). You can also set breakpoints in the debug sources, use conditional breakpoints, or add debugger; statements temporarily. All this is for analysis only: production code must not rely on global lookups. The fastest trick: select an element in the DevTools Elements panel, then type jQuery($0).control(0) in the console to get the UI5 control that rendered it ($0 is the selected DOM element). From there everything is reachable: getMetadata().getName() (the control class), getBindingContext().getPath() (the data row), getModel("i18n"), getParent(), and you can even change something live with setText() or setVisible(false). Useful breakpoint targets when you do not know where to start: Control.prototype.invalidate (why does this re-render?), the model's request methods (what request is being built?), and the router's parse method (why did routing go there?). It is investigation, not development: answer a question in ten seconds instead of adding a console.log, rebuilding and reloading.
keyPoints: In app code use this.byId(); global lookups are for console debugging only.
sap.ui.core.Element.getElementById("fullId") returns a control by its full ID (sap.ui.getCore().byId is deprecated).
Then inspect it: getText(), getBindingContext().getObject(), getModel().getData(), getBinding("items").
sap.ui.require("name") returns already loaded modules; combine with breakpoints in debug sources.
jQuery($0).control(0) returns the control of the DOM element selected in DevTools.

questions.title: What logging possibilities does UI5 offer?
questions.description: UI5 has its own logging module, sap/base/Log (it replaces the deprecated jQuery.sap.log). It offers one method per severity: Log.fatal, Log.error, Log.warning, Log.info, Log.debug and Log.trace, each taking a message, optional details, and a component name (usually the module name), so you can see where an entry comes from. The levels, from least to most detailed, are NONE, FATAL, ERROR, WARNING, INFO, DEBUG, TRACE and ALL. Only entries at or above the current log level are recorded; the default is usually ERROR in production and higher in debug mode. You can raise the level in code with Log.setLevel(Log.Level.DEBUG), optionally only for one component, or with the configuration option for the log level (for example the URL parameter sap-ui-logLevel=DEBUG). Log entries are written to the browser console and kept in memory, where Log.getLogEntries() returns them, and the support tools can show them. UI5 itself logs useful messages, for example about failed bindings, missing i18n texts or deprecated APIs, so raising the log level is often the first step in troubleshooting. Use logging for technical information, never console.log in production code, and never log sensitive data. The signature is (message, details, component); the component (third argument) is what makes the log readable in a large app. By default the level is ERROR, so Log.debug() calls cost almost nothing in production, but are available when you raise the level to investigate.
keyPoints: sap/base/Log: fatal, error, warning, info, debug, trace (message, details, component).
Levels: NONE, FATAL, ERROR, WARNING, INFO, DEBUG, TRACE, ALL; only entries at or above the current level are recorded.
Raise the level with Log.setLevel(...) (per component possible) or the log level config (sap-ui-logLevel).
Entries go to the console and memory (Log.getLogEntries()); no console.log or sensitive data in production.
Default level ERROR: debug logs are free in production and available on demand (sap-ui-logLevel=DEBUG).

questions.title: What is content density?
questions.description: Content density decides how large and how far apart controls are. SAPUI5 has two main densities. Cozy is the default: controls are bigger, with more space between them, so they are easy to hit with a finger on touch devices (buttons are about 2.75rem high). Compact makes controls smaller and denser (buttons about 2rem high), so more information fits on the screen, which suits desktop use with a mouse and keyboard. A third option, condensed, makes table cells even denser, and is used together with compact. Density is switched on by adding the CSS class sapUiSizeCompact or sapUiSizeCozy to a container, usually the app's root view, so it applies to all controls inside. A common pattern is to choose it based on the device, for example compact when Device.support.touch is false. In the manifest, sap.ui5/contentDensities declares which densities the app supports (compact: true, cozy: true); in the SAP Fiori launchpad, the shell then applies the density chosen by the user in their settings. Popups like dialogs are rendered outside the view, so they must get the same class: use sap/ui/core/syncStyleClass("sapUiSizeCompact", view, dialog), or add the class to the dialog. The trap everyone hits: dialogs and popovers are rendered in the static area, so they do not inherit the class; forget it and the dialog is cozy while the app behind it is compact, which is visibly inconsistent and a classic review finding. sapUiSizeCondensed is for sap.ui.table only, always together with compact.
keyPoints: Cozy (default): larger controls for touch; compact: smaller, denser, for mouse and keyboard.
Set with the CSS class sapUiSizeCompact / sapUiSizeCozy on a container, usually the root view.
Often chosen by device (Device.support.touch); declared in the manifest's contentDensities.
The launchpad applies the user's choice; dialogs need syncStyleClass or the class added.
Classic finding: a cozy dialog in a compact app; add the density class (or syncStyleClass) to every dialog.

questions.title: What are the basics of the SAP Fiori launchpad: the shell bar and tiles with their types?
questions.description: The SAP Fiori launchpad is the single entry point for SAP Fiori apps: users log in once and start all their apps from one home page, on desktop and mobile. Its frame is the shell, which stays the same for every app. The shell bar (shell header) at the top shows the company logo and the current app's title, a back button for navigation, a search, notifications, and the user menu (with settings like language, theme and content density, and logout). Apps run inside the shell, which also handles navigation between apps (cross-app navigation by intents). The home page shows tiles, organized in spaces and pages (the newer concept) or in groups (the older one). A tile is the visual entry to an app; when the user clicks it, the launchpad resolves its intent (semantic object and action, like SalesOrder-manage) through a target mapping, and starts the app. Tile types: static tiles show fixed information (title, subtitle, icon); dynamic tiles also show a number that is read from a service, like the count of open orders, refreshed regularly; custom tiles have their own implementation; and there are special ones like news tiles, KPI tiles from analytical content, or links (shown as text only). Which tiles a user sees depends on the catalogs and roles assigned to them. The important architectural point: the shell bar belongs to the launchpad, not to your app; the app renders inside it (in a component container, or in an iframe in some launchpads), which is also why the launchpad has its own back button. The App Finder is where users find apps they are entitled to but have not put on their home page, and newer launchpads (SAP Build Work Zone) also offer cards (list, chart or table previews). The critical technical point: a tile does not point to a URL but to an intent, like #Product-display; the target mapping turns the intent into an app, and that indirection lets an app move, be replaced, or exist in several versions without touching a single tile.
keyPoints: The launchpad is the single entry point for Fiori apps, with one shell around all apps.
Shell bar: logo, title, back, search, notifications, user menu (settings, logout).
The home page shows tiles in spaces and pages (or older groups); clicking resolves an intent via a target mapping.
Tile types: static, dynamic (number from a service), custom, news, KPI, and links; visibility comes from roles and catalogs.
The shell bar belongs to the launchpad; tiles point to intents (not URLs), resolved by target mappings.

examples.title: A dynamic tile's configuration (simplified)
examples.code:
Tile type:     Dynamic
Title:         Open orders
Icon:          sap-icon://sales-order
Service URL:   /sap/opu/odata/sap/ZSALES_SRV/Orders/$count?$filter=Status eq 'O'
Refresh:       every 60 seconds

questions.title: What is the VizFrame, which basic chart types are there, and how does data binding work for charts?
questions.description: sap.viz.ui5.controls.VizFrame is the main chart control of SAPUI5 (in the sap.viz library, available in SAPUI5, not in OpenUI5). Its vizType property selects the chart type. Basic types and their purpose: column and bar (compare values across categories; bar is horizontal, good for long labels), stacked_column and stacked_bar (show parts of a total per category), line (trends over time), pie and donut (parts of a whole, for a few categories only), scatter and bubble (relationships between two or three measures), combination (columns and a line together), and heatmap. Data binding works through a dataset: a sap.viz.ui5.data.FlattenedDataset, which is bound to a collection, like data="{/Sales}", and declares dimensions (the categories, like Month or Region, from DimensionDefinition with a value binding) and measures (the numbers, like Revenue, from MeasureDefinition). Then feeds (sap.viz.ui5.controls. common.feeds.FeedItem) connect them to the chart's axes: for example uid valueAxis for the measures and uid categoryAxis for the dimensions (pies use size and color). Visual details are set with vizProperties, like titles, colors, and data labels. Newer apps can also use sap.suite.ui.microchart for small charts, or analytical charts generated by SAP Fiori elements. More chart types and their purpose: 100% stacked (proportions when the total does not matter), timeseries line, treemap (hierarchy and relative size), waterfall (how a value is built up step by step), and bullet (actual against target). The design rule worth stating: a pie chart with more than five slices is unreadable, so use a bar chart. In the OData V4 world, sap.fe.macros.Chart and sap.ui.mdc.Chart are annotation-driven (UI.Chart) and are what a Fiori elements analytical list page uses.
keyPoints: VizFrame (sap.viz, SAPUI5 only) draws charts; vizType selects the type.
Types: column/bar (compare), stacked (parts of totals), line (trends), pie/donut (share), scatter/bubble, combination.
FlattenedDataset bound to a collection, with dimensions (categories) and measures (numbers).
FeedItems connect them to axes (valueAxis, categoryAxis; size/color for pies); vizProperties for visuals.
Rule: no pie chart with more than five slices. V4 / annotation-driven: sap.fe.macros.Chart (UI.Chart).

examples.title: A column chart
examples.code:
<viz:VizFrame
  xmlns:viz="sap.viz.ui5.controls"
  xmlns:viz.data="sap.viz.ui5.data"
  xmlns:viz.feeds="sap.viz.ui5.controls.common.feeds"
  vizType="column"
  width="100%"
  height="25rem"
  vizProperties="{ title: { text: 'Revenue by month' } }">
  <viz:dataset>
    <viz.data:FlattenedDataset data="{/Sales}">
      <viz.data:dimensions>
        <viz.data:DimensionDefinition name="Month" value="{Month}" />
      </viz.data:dimensions>
      <viz.data:measures>
        <viz.data:MeasureDefinition name="Revenue" value="{Revenue}" />
      </viz.data:measures>
    </viz.data:FlattenedDataset>
  </viz:dataset>
  <viz:feeds>
    <viz.feeds:FeedItem uid="valueAxis" type="Measure" values="Revenue" />
    <viz.feeds:FeedItem uid="categoryAxis" type="Dimension" values="Month" />
  </viz:feeds>
</viz:VizFrame>

questions.title: Which troubleshooting techniques for apps does the documentation recommend?
questions.description: When an app does not work as expected, a systematic approach saves time. First, look at the browser console: UI5 logs errors and warnings there (failed module loads, binding problems, missing i18n texts, deprecated APIs), and raising the log level shows more. Second, check the Network tab: are files or OData requests failing (404, 403, 500), and what do the responses and the $batch contents say? Often the error message comes from the back end. Third, use the UI5-specific tools: the Technical Information dialog (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+P) shows the UI5 version, libraries, and configuration, and can switch on debug sources; the UI5 Inspector shows the control tree and, importantly, the bindings, so you can see whether a control has a model, the right binding context, and the expected path; the Support Assistant checks the app against known rules and points to typical mistakes. Then debug in the readable sources with breakpoints. For common symptoms there are typical causes: an empty list often means a wrong path, a missing model name, or a missing binding context; "resource could not be loaded" usually means a wrong namespace or resource root; a blank page often means an error in the Component or manifest. Finally, rule out caching (old preload, browser or server cache) by testing with sap-ui-xx-componentPreload=off or a clean cache, and reduce the problem to a minimal example if needed. Reading the network tab: a 400 usually means, for example, a filter on a non-filterable field, a 403 usually the CSRF token or a missing authorization, and a 404 a wrong path. Open the $batch payload, because the single requests are inside it. Also open $metadata in the browser: is the field really called that, is the entity set really named that, is it filterable? Isolate the layer: if the problem still happens with mock data, it is the front end; if not, it is the service or the data. On ABAP, check /IWFND/ERROR_LOG and test the service in /IWFND/GW_CLIENT. The principle to state: narrow it down before changing anything; is it the UI, the binding, the request, the service or the data? Changing code before you know which layer is broken is how an afternoon disappears.
keyPoints: Check the console (UI5 errors and warnings, raise the log level) and the Network tab (failed requests, back-end messages).
Use Technical Information, debug sources, the UI5 Inspector (bindings!), and the Support Assistant.
Typical causes: empty list = wrong path / model name / context; load errors = wrong namespace or resource roots.
Rule out caching (preload off, clean caches) and reduce to a minimal example.
Network: 400 = bad query (e.g. non-filterable field), 403 = CSRF/authorization, 404 = wrong path; check $metadata.
Isolate with mock data (front end vs service); narrow down the layer before changing code.

examples.title: A quick checklist for an empty table
examples.code:
1. Console: any binding or loading errors?
2. Network: was the OData request sent? Status 200? Does the response contain data?
3. UI5 Inspector: does the table have the model? Is the items binding path correct ("/Products")?
4. Named model? Then the path needs the prefix: items="{product>/Products}"
5. Relative path? Then the parent needs a binding context (bindElement)

questions.title: What is the reuse library approach?
questions.description: When several apps need the same controls, fragments, formatters, or helper modules, copying them into every app leads to duplicated code that drifts apart and must be fixed in many places. A reuse library solves this: the shared code is put into a UI5 library (a project of type library, with a library.js that calls Lib.init with the library's name, version, dependencies and the controls it contains), which is built and deployed once, and then used by all apps. A consuming app declares the library as a dependency in its manifest, under sap.ui5/dependencies/libs (for example "my.shared.lib": {}, with lazy: true if it should be loaded only when needed), and then uses its modules and controls like any UI5 library, through their namespace. In development, the UI5 tooling resolves the library through package dependencies or a workspace configuration; in the deployed system, the library is a separate deployment (for example a BSP application or an HTML5 app on SAP BTP), and the platform makes it available, sometimes with resourceRoots or app index information. Benefits are one place to fix and improve shared code, consistent behavior across apps, and smaller apps. The costs are versioning and compatibility: changes to the library affect every app, so it needs its own tests, a stable API, and careful releases. A typical structure is src/<namespace>/ with .library, library.js, a manifest.json of type library, the controls, shared formatters and fragments, and a messagebundle.properties, plus ui5.yaml with type: library; the build creates a library-preload.js. Good content for a library: custom controls, shared formatters and data types, shared fragments, a shared BaseController and utility classes. It must be deployed to every platform the apps run on (a BSP application on ABAP, the HTML5 repository or a private npm registry on SAP BTP). The lighter alternative is a reuse component: a whole UI5 component embedded in another app, declared under componentUsages in the manifest and created with createComponent(). Use a component to reuse a whole screen or flow, and a library to reuse building blocks.
keyPoints: A reuse library holds shared controls, fragments, formatters and helpers for many apps.
It is a library project (library.js with Lib.init), built and deployed once.
Apps declare it in sap.ui5/dependencies/libs (optionally lazy) and use it through its namespace.
Benefits: one place to fix, consistency; costs: versioning and compatibility, so test and release carefully.
Reuse component (componentUsages + createComponent) for whole screens; library for building blocks.

<mvc:View xmlns="sap.m" xmlns:mvc="sap.ui.core.mvc" xmlns:shared="my.shared.lib">
  <shared:StatusBadge text="{StatusText}" status="{Status}" />
</mvc:View>

questions.title: What are the ways to transfer data between pages of an app?
questions.description: There are several ways, and the right one depends on what the data is. Route parameters are the first choice for identifying what a page shows: navTo("detail", { orderId: "4711" }) puts the ID into the URL hash, and the detail page reads it in its route-matched handler and loads or binds the data. This way, the page works after a reload, from a bookmark, and from a shared link; pass only IDs and small values this way, never whole objects. Shared models are the second option: a model set on the Component (in the manifest or with this.setModel) is visible in every view, so a page can write a value (like the current selection or filter settings) and another page can read or bind to it. With an OData model, both pages naturally share the same cached data, so the detail page often only needs the key. The event bus lets one page publish an event that another page subscribes to, which is useful for notifications like "data has changed, refresh", but not for state that must survive a reload. Across apps in the SAP Fiori launchpad, data is passed with intent parameters (cross-app navigation) and, for larger states, with app state services. Avoid global variables and passing data through the controller instances of other views. The anti-pattern to name: passing a whole object through a router parameter or a global variable. The URL gets long, and when the user reloads the page the object is gone and the app shows an empty screen; pass the key and re-read the data. Browser storage (sap/ui/util/Storage) is only for something like a draft the user should find again after closing the browser, never for business or sensitive data.
keyPoints: Route parameters (in the hash) for IDs and small values: reload- and bookmark-safe.
Shared models on the Component for state used by several pages; OData pages share the model cache.
The event bus for notifications between pages, not for lasting state.
Across apps: intent parameters and app state; avoid globals and reaching into other controllers.
Anti-pattern: whole objects in the hash or in globals; pass the key, re-read the data.

examples.title: Passing an ID and sharing state

questions.title: What are the device adaptation aspects of an SAPUI5 app?
questions.description: SAPUI5 apps run on desktops, tablets and phones, so they must adapt to the device. Most of this comes from responsive controls, which adapt their layout by themselves: sap.m.Table with pop-in, forms with ColumnLayout, DynamicPage, FlexibleColumnLayout, OverflowToolbar, and the responsive margin and padding classes. For your own decisions, sap/ui/Device provides information about the device: Device.system.phone, tablet, desktop (and combi for touch laptops), Device.support.touch, Device.browser, Device.os, Device.orientation (portrait or landscape), and Device.resize with the current window size. Device.media lets you react to screen-width ranges (like the standard Phone, Tablet, Desktop range set) with attachHandler. The common pattern is a device model: a JSONModel created from the Device object in the Component (one-way), so views can bind to it, like visible="{= !${device>/system/phone} }" or mode="{= ${device>/system/phone} ? 'None' : 'SingleSelectMaster' }". Other aspects are the content density (compact for mouse, cozy for touch), the manifest's sap.ui/deviceTypes (which devices the app supports), touch-friendly interaction (no hover-only features), and performance on mobile devices and slow networks. Always test on real small screens or with the browser's device emulation. Remember to detach Device.media, Device.orientation and Device.resize handlers in onExit, or you have a leak. Adaptation also means hiding non-essential functions, like an Excel export that makes little sense on a phone. The principle to state: prefer responsive design over device detection; let the responsive controls and CSS handle the layout, and use Device only for decisions CSS cannot make, like content density, whether to show a function at all, or which control to create.
keyPoints: Responsive controls (Table pop-in, ColumnLayout forms, DynamicPage, FCL, OverflowToolbar) adapt by themselves.
sap/ui/Device: system (phone/tablet/desktop/combi), support.touch, browser, os, orientation, resize, media ranges.
A one-way device model lets views bind to device information.
Also: content density, manifest deviceTypes, no hover-only features, mobile performance, real-device testing.
Prefer responsive controls over device detection; detach Device handlers in onExit.

questions.title: How does message handling work: the message model, Messaging (MessageManager), and validation messages from the back end and the UI?
questions.description: UI5 has a central place for messages (errors, warnings, information, success), so that they can be collected from everywhere and shown in one consistent way. The central module is sap/ui/core/Messaging (since 1.118; it replaces the deprecated sap.ui.getCore().getMessageManager()). It holds all messages, each an sap.ui.core.message.Message with a type (Error, Warning, Success, Information), a message text, a description, and a target, the binding path of the field it belongs to, like /Orders('1')/Quantity. Messaging.getMessageModel() returns a message model (sap.ui.model.message.MessageModel) that contains all of them, which is usually set on the view or component under the name message, so controls can bind to it. Messages come from two sources. From the back end: the OData model reads messages that the server sends (the sap-message header for warnings and information on successful requests, and the error details of failed requests) and adds them automatically, with their targets. From the UI: when a data type's parse or validation fails (for example letters in a number field, or a value below a minimum), a validation message is created; for this, validation handling must be switched on, with "handleValidation": true in the manifest's sap.ui5 section, or Messaging.registerObject(view, true). Messages with a target are shown directly on the bound field as a value state (red or orange frame with the text), and they are removed when the value becomes valid again. Your own code can add messages with Messaging.addMessages. In OData V4, back-end messages arrive in the payload (the SAP__Messages annotation of an entity) or in the error body, and the V4 model adds them to the message model with their targets too. Because a target matches a binding path, the right field turns red automatically, without front-end mapping code. Message types are Error, Warning, Success, Information and None. The related controls, for a complete answer: MessageBox (a modal dialog for a decision or a blocking error), MessageToast (a short non-blocking confirmation like "Saved"), MessageStrip (an inline banner in the page) and MessagePopover (the list). SAP Fiori elements does all of this out of the box; knowing the manual implementation is what lets you understand and extend it.
keyPoints: sap/ui/core/Messaging (since 1.118, replaces the MessageManager) collects all messages centrally.
A Message has type, text, description, and a target (binding path of a field).
Back-end messages come via the OData model (sap-message header, error responses); UI messages from type validation.
handleValidation: true (or registerObject) turns on UI validation messages; targeted messages show as value states.
V4: messages from SAP__Messages / error bodies; targets match binding paths, so fields turn red automatically.
MessageBox (modal), MessageToast (confirmation), MessageStrip (inline), MessagePopover (list).

questions.title: How do you show messages with a message button in the footer and a message popover?
questions.description: The SAP Fiori design pattern for showing many messages on a page is a message button on the left side of the footer, together with a message popover. The button (an sap.m.Button) shows the number of messages, and its type and icon reflect the most severe message: Negative with an error icon when there are errors, Critical for warnings, and so on. It is visible only when there are messages. Pressing it opens an sap.m.MessagePopover (or an sap.m.MessageView inside a dialog), whose items (sap.m.MessageItem) are bound to the message model, like items="{message>/}", with title, subtitle, description, and type from each message. The popover groups or filters the messages by type, and for messages with a target, an item can navigate to the field it belongs to, with activeTitle and the activeTitlePress event, which sets the focus on that field. This pattern works together with message handling: all messages from the back end and from validation end up in the message model, so the button and the popover always show the current state without extra code. SAP Fiori elements apps provide this pattern automatically.
keyPoints: A message button in the footer (left) shows the count; its type/icon reflect the most severe message.
It opens a MessagePopover (or MessageView) whose MessageItems are bound to the message model.
Items show title, subtitle, description, and type; activeTitlePress can focus the related field.
With message handling active, button and popover always reflect the current messages.

examples.title: Footer button and message popover
examples.code:
<footer>
  <OverflowToolbar>
    <Button
      icon="sap-icon://message-error"
      type="Negative"
      text="{= ${message>/}.length }"
      visible="{= ${message>/}.length > 0 }"
      press=".onOpenMessages" />
    <ToolbarSpacer />
    <Button text="Save" type="Emphasized" press=".onSave" />
  </OverflowToolbar>
</footer>

<!-- MessagePopover.fragment.xml -->

questions.title: What is a target mapping?
questions.description: In the SAP Fiori launchpad, apps are not started by their URL, but by an intent: a semantic object (the business entity, like SalesOrder or Product) plus an action (what to do with it, like display, manage, or create), written as #SalesOrder-manage. A target mapping is the configuration that connects an intent to the actual app that should be started. It defines the semantic object and action, and the target: for a UI5 app, the component (its ID, like my.sales.orders) and where it is deployed (for example the BSP application's URL or the SAP BTP app); it also defines which device types it supports, and parameters (default values, and whether additional parameters are allowed). Tiles and links only reference an intent; the launchpad resolves the intent through the target mapping, so the same intent can lead to different apps for different users or devices, and the app can be exchanged without touching the tiles. Target mappings are created in catalogs, with the launchpad content tools (like the launchpad designer or the app descriptor-based content in SAP BTP); the user must have a role that includes the catalog. In the app, the matching inbound is declared in manifest.json under sap.app/crossNavigation/inbounds. Cross-app navigation between apps also uses intents, resolved through target mappings. The target can be an SAPUI5 component, a URL, an SAP GUI transaction or a Web Dynpro application, so #SalesOrder-display may even open transaction VA03 through the Web GUI. Why the indirection exists: tiles and links keep working when an app moves or a BSP is renamed; cross-app navigation works without hard-coded URLs (an app says "navigate to Product-display with ProductID HT-1000" and the launchpad resolves it); different roles can be mapped to different implementations of the same intent; and SmartLinks (Common.SemanticObject) build their list of navigation targets from the target mappings the user may use. On ABAP it is configured in the launchpad designer or LPD_CUST, on SAP BTP in SAP Build Work Zone. In code, navigation goes through the launchpad's navigation service (the older CrossApplicationNavigation service with toExternal, or the newer Navigation service with navigate in current UI5 versions).
keyPoints: Launchpad apps are started by intents: semantic object + action, like #SalesOrder-manage.
A target mapping connects an intent to the actual app (component ID and deployment), per device type, with parameters.
Tiles and links reference only the intent, so the app can be exchanged without touching tiles.
Created in catalogs (user needs a role); the app declares inbounds in sap.app/crossNavigation.
Targets: UI5 component, URL, SAP GUI transaction, Web Dynpro. Roles can map one intent to different apps.
SmartLinks read the target mappings; navigate in code with the launchpad navigation service.

questions.title: What is the event bus, and what are its use cases?
questions.description: The event bus (sap.ui.core.EventBus) is a simple publish and subscribe mechanism: one part of the app publishes an event on a channel, and any number of other parts that subscribed to that channel and event name are called, without knowing each other. This decouples parts that have no direct reference to each other. The recommended instance is the component's event bus, this.getOwnerComponent().getEventBus(), which is limited to one component and destroyed with it; the global instance (EventBus.getInstance()) affects the whole page and should be used rarely. You call subscribe(channelId, eventId, handler, listener) to listen, publish(channelId, eventId, data) to send an event with data, and unsubscribe with the same arguments to stop listening, which must be done (for example in onExit), or the handler keeps running on destroyed views. Use cases: notifying other views that data changed ("order saved, refresh the list"), communication between a component and nested components, or between parts of a layout like the columns of a FlexibleColumnLayout. It should not be used to pass lasting state (use models for that) or as a replacement for normal method calls and routing, because event flows that are too loose make an app hard to follow and debug. The handler signature is (sChannelId, sEventId, oData): the data is the third argument, which is easy to get wrong. More use cases are app-wide notifications, like the session is about to expire or a background job finished. The caveats matter as much as the use cases: it hides dependencies (you cannot see who listens without searching for the channel name), a missing subscription fails silently, and a missing unsubscribe keeps the destroyed controller alive (a memory leak and often a "cannot read property of null" error later). Keep channel and event names as constants in one module. Prefer a shared model, routing parameters or a direct method call when they fit; the event bus is the right answer only when there genuinely is no reference between the two sides.
keyPoints: The event bus is publish/subscribe: publishers and subscribers do not know each other.
Prefer the component's bus (getOwnerComponent().getEventBus()); the global instance affects the whole page.
subscribe(channel, event, handler, listener), publish(channel, event, data), unsubscribe (in onExit!).
Use for notifications ("data changed"), component communication; not for lasting state or instead of routing.
Handler signature (channel, event, data); keep names as constants; it hides dependencies and fails silently.
